idiom_name: duck typing with respond_to? plus mixin modules (Comparable, Enumerable)
implementation_notes: In Ruby the property that decides behaviour is whether an object responds to a message: respond_to? is the runtime predicate, and the mixin modules are the retroactive half of a descriptor - include Comparable plus a single <=> definition gives the class <, <=, ==, >=, >, between? and clamp, and Enumerable derives a whole protocol from each. Describing a type you do not own is possible because classes are open (reopening, Module#prepend) and refine scopes such changes lexically. The classic descriptor itself has no counterpart because a class carries no per-type constants or associated types: a property is either a method (define it in a module) or a convention (obj.is_a?, obj.respond_to?, obj.class).
code_sketch:
module LengthKeyed
  def <=>(other) = size <=> other.size    # one primitive...
end
class Frame
  include Comparable                      # ...derives <, <=, ==, >, >=, between?, clamp
  include LengthKeyed
  def size = @bytes.length
end

def describe(obj)                          # property check instead of a type test
  obj.respond_to?(:each) ? obj.each.to_a.inspect : obj.to_s
end
pitfalls: respond_to? is only honest for delegators/proxies if they also implement respond_to_missing?; without it a decorated object reports false for every forwarded method and the property check takes the wrong branch.
Comparison derived from <=> fails quietly: if <=> returns nil (incomparable) the derived operators return false instead of raising, so ordering bugs surface far from the definition.

Reopening a shared class to attach behaviour is global for the process, collides across gems, and cannot be done for frozen classes or objects; use refine (lexically scoped) or include the module in the class definition when the type is yours.
